title: Procurement + Legal: measurement of usage / billing disputes (Redwood Inference)
summary: Customer procurement and legal team asked how Redwood measures usage for Hosted API vs Dedicated/VPC options, how token accounting works (input/output, streaming, retries), and what the dispute/audit process looks like. Redwood aligned on: meter definitions come from request-level telemetry; invoices are derived from aggregated, versioned meters; streaming is billed only for tokens actually generated before disconnect; retries are handled via outcome/retry dimensions so failed/non-billable paths are excluded per contract language. Legal discussed dispute window and audit rights; Finance discussed what artifacts Redwood can provide during a dispute (request IDs, usage exports, invoice line-item mapping). Next steps: Redwood to share the approved 'measurement and billing' clause language, an example invoice mapped to usage export fields, and a short written explainer on streaming/retry edge cases; customer to send redlines and confirm preferred dispute window language.
topics: Measurement definitions; token meters (input/output); streaming disconnects; retries/failed requests; rounding and aggregation windows; hosted vs dedicated attribution; dispute window; audit rights and evidence; console vs invoice alignment; data retention of request logs; security boundaries for VPC/private deployments
questions: What exactly is a 'token' for billing (prompt vs completion, tool calls)?; If a client disconnects mid-stream do you still bill the remainder?; How do you treat retries/timeouts/429s?; Can we dispute a specific line item with request IDs?; What is the dispute window (30/60/90 days) and do we have audit rights?; Can we get monthly usage exports with dimensions (model, region, endpoint)?; How does Dedicated commit burn-down map to invoice?

Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Procurement + Legal: measurement of usage / billing disputes (Redwood Inference)
Date: 2026-01-14
Time: 10:30 AM PT
Duration: 47 minutes

Attendees
- Isabelle Laurent (Redwood) 
- Sofia Mendes (Redwood) 
- Emily Stone (Redwood)
- Anika Rao (NorthBridge, Procurement)
- Daniel Cho (NorthBridge, Legal)
- Priya Desai (NorthBridge, Security/GRC)
- Mark Ellison (NorthBridge, Platform Eng)

---

[Auto Summary]
Customer wants clarity on how usage is measured and what happens when they dispute charges. Discussion covered token definitions, streaming partials/disconnects, retries and failed requests, rounding/aggregation cadence, and the difference between Hosted API and Dedicated commit attribution. Redwood agreed to share clause language and a redacted example mapping invoice line items to telemetry/usage exports.

---

[00:00] Isabelle Laurent: Alright, I think we’ve got everybody. Thanks for making the time. This is Isabelle from Redwood. I’m joined by Sofia from our commercial legal team and Emily from finance, who helps us with billing controls.

[00:12] Anika Rao: Great, thanks Isabelle. Yeah, we wanted to do this before we get too far in procurement. The big thing is measurement. Like, how do you measure usage and how do we dispute it if there’s a mismatch.

[00:23] Daniel Cho: And related, our template has specific audit rights language. We need to see what you can reasonably provide.

[00:30] Isabelle Laurent: Totally. Maybe we start with the practical side, then Sofia can speak to the clause language and dispute window.

[00:38] Emily Stone: Yep. And I can cover what’s on the invoice, what’s in the console, and what artifacts we can produce if you have a question on a line item.

[00:46] Mark Ellison: I’m mostly here to understand token accounting. We’ve had issues with other providers where the console says one thing and the invoice says another.

[00:55] Isabelle Laurent: Makes sense. Quick framing: for Hosted API we bill based on usage meters—primarily tokens and request types. For Dedicated it’s generally commit-based with usage attribution for burn-down and overages depending on the structure.

[01:09] Priya Desai: And for VPC, do you even see our data? Like are you logging prompts?

[01:14] Isabelle Laurent: Good question. For Private/VPC deployments we can configure what telemetry is captured. We always need enough to measure the meters, but you can set retention and whether payloads are stored. We can get into that later, but today is more measurement + disputes.

[01:28] Daniel Cho: Let’s start with: what is a token in your definition?

[01:31] Emily Stone: Sure. For text generation/chat we meter input tokens (prompt) and output tokens (completion). Those are counted by the tokenizer for the specific model family. We also have meters for embeddings and reranking—those are separate units because the workload is different.

[01:49] Mark Ellison: Model-specific tokenizer meaning… the same text could be different tokens across models.

[01:54] Emily Stone: Correct. And that’s why the invoice line items include model or model family. The usage export includes a model identifier so it’s explainable.

[02:03] Anika Rao: Okay. How about tool calls or function calling? Is that billed as output tokens?

[02:09] Emily Stone: Generally yes—anything the model generates as part of completion is output tokens. If it’s structured output, it still counts. We don’t have a separate surcharge for tool calling. You’ll see it reflected in the output token count.

[02:22] Daniel Cho: What about retries or failed requests? Like timeouts, 500 errors, rate limiting. Do we get billed?

[02:29] Emily Stone: Not in a blanket way. The metering pipeline has request outcome. If there’s an error before generation, there should be zero output tokens. If a request fails after partial generation, we only count tokens generated up to that point.

[02:45] Mark Ellison: That gets into streaming. If the client disconnects—say the user closes the tab—do you still keep generating and bill us?

[02:54] Emily Stone: No. We stop billing at disconnect. The metered output tokens should represent what was actually produced and delivered before disconnect. If there’s a disconnect event, tokens after that are not billable.

[03:08] Mark Ellison: How do you know what was delivered versus generated?

[03:12] Emily Stone: It’s based on the stream lifecycle events. The server tracks the stream and marks the last acknowledged chunk. I want to be careful on implementation details, but from a billing perspective: billed streaming output is capped to the tokens generated prior to termination.

[03:30] Daniel Cho: Is that a policy in the contract or just best effort?

[03:35] Sofia Mendes: In our measurement language we describe that usage is measured based on our systems and logs, and we include definitions for billable units. We can add clarifying language for streaming and failed requests. Typically we say: you’re billed for successful processing and usage consumed, and we’ll exclude usage attributable to Redwood system errors. Client-side disconnects are treated as partial fulfillment—billed to the extent provided.

[04:02] Anika Rao: We’d want that spelled out. “Partial fulfillment billed to extent provided” is okay as long as it’s not like “we attempted.”

[04:10] Sofia Mendes: Agreed. We can word it as “actually generated and transmitted prior to termination” rather than “attempted.”

[04:18] Isabelle Laurent: And Emily will share a one-pager that explains those edge cases in plain language. It helps support teams on both sides.

[04:27] Priya Desai: You mentioned console versus invoice. Can you explain how those align? Because if our engineers are watching spend in the console, we can’t have a surprise invoice.

[04:38] Emily Stone: Yeah. Console usage is the same underlying aggregation as invoicing, but time windows can cause confusion—like time zone cutoffs, and sometimes rounding rules if people export daily numbers and sum them up. Our invoicing aggregates at the monthly window and applies rounding at the aggregated level, not per request.

[04:57] Mark Ellison: Wait—so you don’t round each request?

[04:59] Emily Stone: Correct. We aggregate tokens in the billing window and then round at the line-item level. That prevents systematic over-rounding.

[05:08] Daniel Cho: That’s good. We’ve seen per-request rounding inflate invoices.

[05:13] Emily Stone: Yeah. It’s a known anti-pattern. We avoid it.

[05:18] Anika Rao: Okay. Disputes: If we think an invoice is wrong, what do we do? Do we have to pay first and dispute later, or can we pause payment?

[05:28] Sofia Mendes: Standard approach: you notify us within a dispute window—often 30 days from invoice date, sometimes 60 for enterprise. You pay the undisputed portion on time. For disputed amounts, we work in good faith to reconcile. We can discuss whether a disputed portion can be withheld depending on your policy.

[05:50] Daniel Cho: Our template has 90 days and also has audit rights—once per year, with a third-party auditor, under NDA.

[06:00] Sofia Mendes: We’re generally open to reasonable audit rights, but for a usage-based API it’s tricky because raw logs include other customers’ system details, and also potentially sensitive info. What we usually do is provide audit evidence artifacts—usage exports, invoice line-item mapping, and sample request IDs—rather than opening our entire systems.

[06:23] Daniel Cho: Understood. But we need some mechanism.

[06:26] Sofia Mendes: Yep. We can propose language: you can audit the accuracy of charges via review of mutually agreed records and reports, and we’ll provide supporting documentation. If you need third-party involvement, we can limit scope to billing records, under confidentiality, no penetration testing, that sort of thing.

[06:44] Priya Desai: From security standpoint, we also need to know what logs you retain, especially if PHI could ever be in prompts.

[06:52] Isabelle Laurent: For regulated workloads, we typically recommend Private/VPC where you have tighter control. For Hosted, we have data retention settings and can disable payload storage; metadata for billing is retained longer for auditability.

[07:08] Mark Ellison: Metadata meaning request IDs, token counts, model name, timestamps…

[07:12] Emily Stone: Exactly. Like customer org ID, workspace, model, region, endpoint type, input/output tokens, and outcome codes. Not necessarily the content.

[07:23] Anika Rao: Can you provide that export monthly, automatically?

[07:27] Emily Stone: Yes, we can provide a CSV or JSON export. Some customers pull it via API. We can align on the fields you need—model, region, project, whatever dimensions are enabled.

[07:41] Daniel Cho: If there’s a dispute, what’s the process? Do you have an escalation path?

[07:46] Isabelle Laurent: Yes. Support can intake the case, then it goes to our telemetry/billing team for reconciliation. We typically ask for a date range, any request IDs you have, and what you’re comparing against. We can then reconcile raw telemetry aggregates to billing aggregates and identify if it’s a misunderstanding or a defect.

[08:08] Mark Ellison: You said “raw telemetry” — do you keep raw request events?

[08:13] Emily Stone: We retain the event-level meter records with IDs and counts. We also store the billing-ready aggregates that feed the invoice. And we version the meter definitions so if there’s a change, it’s documented.

[08:27] Daniel Cho: Versioned meter definitions—like if you change how you count streaming?

[08:31] Emily Stone: Yes, exactly. Changes that affect invoices are controlled and have cross-functional sign-off.

[08:39] Sofia Mendes: And from a contract perspective, we reference the product documentation for definitions, but we keep the key billing definitions in the agreement as well, to reduce ambiguity.

[08:51] Anika Rao: Can you send us that clause language? We want to compare to our template.

[08:55] Sofia Mendes: Yep. I’ll send our current approved “measurement and billing” section with a couple optional variants for dispute window.

[09:04] Isabelle Laurent: And we can include a redacted example invoice showing how a line item maps to the usage export fields. That’s usually what procurement asks for.

[09:13] Mark Ellison: That would be helpful. Also: caching and batching. If you do caching, does that reduce billed tokens? Or do we get charged regardless?

[09:23] Emily Stone: You’re charged for the billable units as defined. If caching avoids compute, that can affect pricing in some plans or Dedicated economics, but the token meter is still tokens processed. Some customers have separate “cached tokens” meters for optimization insight. Depending on the plan, cached tokens may be priced differently or used for internal reporting.

[09:44] Mark Ellison: So you might have “cached input tokens” as a separate metric.

[09:47] Emily Stone: Yes—again, depends on how the plan is set up. For most standard Hosted pricing, it’s input and output tokens. But in enterprise arrangements, we can break out cached tokens for transparency.

[10:01] Daniel Cho: If you introduce a new meter later, does that change pricing automatically?

[10:05] Sofia Mendes: No, not without an amendment or the order form specifying it. We can update documentation, but charges have to align to the order form and the meter definitions agreed.

[10:17] Anika Rao: That’s important. We’ve seen vendors add “platform fees” after the fact.

[10:21] Isabelle Laurent: Not how we operate. If anything changes, it’s a renewal conversation.

[10:27] Priya Desai: Can we talk dispute window? Our standard is 90 days because invoices sometimes get routed late.

[10:33] Sofia Mendes: I hear you. We can consider 60 days as a middle ground. 90 is sometimes hard because logs and systems change, but given we keep meter records, it might be workable if scoped.

[10:47] Emily Stone: From finance perspective, we can support 60 comfortably. 90 we’d want to ensure we’re not keeping payload data, only meter events.

[10:58] Daniel Cho: Okay. We’ll see your proposed language and respond.

[11:03] Mark Ellison: Another practical: What about timezone? Our finance team wants everything in UTC.

[11:08] Emily Stone: Invoicing is in UTC for the billing window boundaries. Console can display in local time for convenience, but the billing export uses UTC timestamps.

[11:20] Mark Ellison: Good.

[11:22] Anika Rao: Dedicated. We’re not sure if we start Hosted then move to Dedicated, but we want to understand how commit burn-down is measured.

[11:32] Isabelle Laurent: For Dedicated, the commit is typically a monthly dollar amount tied to reserved capacity. Usage attribution is calculated from the same meters, and it burns down against the commit. If you exceed, overage rates apply based on the contract.

[11:48] Mark Ellison: So it’s still token-based behind the scenes.

[11:51] Isabelle Laurent: Usually yes, plus potentially requests/throughput constraints. But the invoice will show commit charge and then any overages.

[12:02] Daniel Cho: Do you ever true-up prior periods if you find a metering bug?

[12:07] Emily Stone: If we find an issue, we correct it and assess impact. Depending on timing, we may issue a credit memo rather than reissuing past invoices. We don’t like surprises either way, so we coordinate.

[12:22] Anika Rao: That’s fine, as long as it’s transparent.

[12:26] Sofia Mendes: And we can add language around adjustments—e.g., if there’s a material error we’ll correct in good faith and notify you.

[12:36] Priya Desai: What’s “material” here?

[12:38] Sofia Mendes: Typically a threshold, or we can leave it as “reasonable” and rely on dispute mechanism. We can discuss.

[12:47] Mark Ellison: Sorry, one more—rate limiting. If we get 429, is that billed?

[12:51] Emily Stone: No, if it’s rejected before processing. 429s generally do not include token processing.

[12:58] Mark Ellison: And if your system errors—like 500.

[13:01] Emily Stone: If it errors before generation, no. If it errors after partial generation, we bill for the portion delivered, but if it’s due to our fault we can credit. That’s where the dispute process and support escalation is used.

[13:19] Daniel Cho: That needs to be clear in contract: “vendor system errors not billed.”

[13:24] Sofia Mendes: Yes, we can include language: charges exclude usage attributable to Redwood’s failure to provide the service. And then define what counts as failure.

[13:35] Isabelle Laurent: I want to respect time. Maybe we do a quick recap and next steps.

[13:41] Anika Rao: Before recap—can you provide an example of the usage export fields? Just a list.

[13:47] Emily Stone: Yes. We’ll include: organization_id, project_id if enabled, request_id, timestamp_utc, model, region, endpoint_type, input_tokens, output_tokens, total_tokens, request_outcome, retry_reason if applicable, and the meter_version. Plus the aggregation window for any summarized exports.

[14:11] Mark Ellison: Perfect.

[14:13] Daniel Cho: And do you provide a mapping from invoice line items to those fields?

[14:17] Emily Stone: Yes. For example: “Hosted API - Text generation - Model X - US-West” maps to model=X, endpoint_type=chat/completions, region=us-west, then sum input/output tokens for the month.

[14:33] Daniel Cho: Great.

[14:35] Isabelle Laurent: Recap: Sofia will send measurement and billing clause language and dispute window options. Emily will send a short metering explainer and field list and an example mapping. I’ll send a redacted sample invoice with a screenshot of how it shows up in our console, so you can see the alignment.

[14:56] Anika Rao: Sounds good.

[14:57] Daniel Cho: We’ll consolidate our redlines and send back.

[15:01] Priya Desai: And I’ll probably have follow-ups on retention and PHI. But this was helpful.

[15:06] Isabelle Laurent: Great. Mark, on Hosted vs VPC, we can do a separate technical/security call. But for now, we’ll wait on your decision for the pilot.

[15:15] Mark Ellison: Yep, we’ll confirm.

[15:18] Isabelle Laurent: Cool. Thanks everyone. We’ll follow up by end of week.

---

[End of transcript]
